title: Checkpoint 6 Maths — Practice Test 1
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Mathematics 0096 · Stage 6 · Practice test
summary: A full timed Checkpoint-style Maths test — Paper 1 without a calculator and Paper 2 with one, 45 minutes and 40 marks each — set in a school library, a juice stall, a zoo trip, a garden plan, sports day and a weather chart, with automatic marking, a mark scheme and full worked solutions.

items: This is a full practice test in the style of the **Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Mathematics (0096)** test, which is taken at the end of Stage 6. It covers the whole Stage 6 curriculum: number, geometry and measure, and statistics and probability.
There are **two papers**. Each paper lasts **45 minutes** and is worth **40 marks** (80 marks in total). The timer starts when you press Start.
**Paper 1: no calculator.** All the numbers are chosen so that you can work them out on paper. **Paper 2: you may use a calculator.** Paper 2 has more real-life, multi-step problems.
**Equipment:** a black or dark blue pen, an HB pencil for drawings, a ruler, compasses and a protractor (tracing paper is optional). Keep some squared paper ready to sketch shapes and grids.
You can **write on paper first** if you like: download the question paper (PDF), do the test the real way, then type in your answers or mark your paper with the mark scheme (PDF).

**How marking works here:** typed answers (numbers, short answers and multiple choice) are checked automatically. Written answers (explanations, drawings, sketches) you mark yourself at the end: compare your answer with the mark scheme and give yourself only the marks you have really earned.
**[2] marks** means "show your working": in the real test a correct method can still earn 1 mark even if the final answer is wrong. Give units (cm², °C, minutes) where they are asked for.
Your score is a **practice score** to show you what to revise. It is **not** an official Cambridge result.

blocks.title: Checkpoint 6 Maths — Practice Test 1
blocks.intro: Two papers, 45 minutes each, 40 marks each. Paper 1: no calculator. Paper 2: calculator allowed. Type coordinates with brackets, for example (2, -1), and fractions with a slash, for example 3/4. Typed answers are marked automatically; written answers and drawings you mark yourself with the mark scheme at the end.

questions.p:
Question 1
The school library counts its books. It has 2 thousands, 15 hundreds, 3 tens and 8 ones.
questions.q: How many books does the library have?
questions.e:
Regroup: 15 hundreds = 1 thousand and 5 hundreds.
2000 + 1500 + 30 + 8 = **3538** books.
Common mistake: writing 21 538 by putting the digits 2, 15, 3, 8 side by side.

questions.p:
Question 2
A sequence counts back in steps of the same size.
2.0,   1.4,   0.8,   ___,   ___
questions.q: Write the next two numbers. Type them with a comma between them, for example 5, 3
questions.e:
The step is 2.0 − 1.4 = 0.6, so subtract 0.6 each time.
0.8 − 0.6 = **0.2**
0.2 − 0.6 = **−0.4** (go past zero: 0.2 takes you to 0, then 0.4 more below zero).
Both numbers are needed for the mark.

questions.p: Question 3
questions.q: (a) Work out  30 − 4 × 6 ÷ 3
questions.e:
Multiplication and division come before subtraction, working from left to right.
4 × 6 = 24, then 24 ÷ 3 = 8.
30 − 8 = **22**.
Common mistake: working left to right from the start: 30 − 4 = 26, × 6 = 156, ÷ 3 = 52.

questions.p: Question 3
questions.q:
(b) Write one pair of brackets to make this calculation correct.
5 + 3 × 4 − 2 = 30
questions.ms: 1 mark: (5 + 3) × 4 − 2 = 30. Accept ((5 + 3) × 4) − 2. Do not accept any other position of the brackets.
questions.e:
Try the brackets in different places:
(5 + 3) × 4 − 2 = 8 × 4 − 2 = 32 − 2 = **30** ✓
5 + 3 × (4 − 2) = 5 + 6 = 11 ✗
(5 + 3) × (4 − 2) uses two pairs, and gives 16 ✗
Without brackets: 5 + 12 − 2 = 15 ✗
So the brackets go around **5 + 3**.

questions.p:
Question 4
A juice stall sells 1245 cups of juice in April.
Each cup costs 24 pounds.
questions.q: How much money does the stall take for these cups in April? Show your working.
questions.e:
Estimate first: 1200 × 25 = 30 000, so the answer is about 30 000.
1245 × 20 = 24 900
1245 × 4 = 4980
24 900 + 4980 = **29 880 pounds**
Mark scheme: M1 for a complete correct method (for example the two partial products 24 900 and 4980, or a grid method) with no more than one arithmetic error; A1 for 29 880.

questions.p:
Question 5
The juice stall has 912 oranges. The oranges are packed into bags of 16.
questions.q: How many bags can be filled? Show your working.
questions.e:
Estimate: 900 ÷ 15 = 60, so the answer is a little under 60.
16 × 50 = 800, leaving 912 − 800 = 112.
16 × 7 = 112, leaving 0.
50 + 7 = **57 bags** (exactly, no oranges left over).
Check: 57 × 16 = 570 + 342 = 912 ✓
Mark scheme: M1 for a correct method (chunking, short or long division) with at most one error; A1 for 57.

questions.p:
Question 6
On a class trip to the zoo, the sea-lion show starts every 15 minutes.
The parrot show starts every 20 minutes.
Both shows start at 10:00
questions.q: What is the next time that both shows start together?
questions.e:
List the start times (minutes after 10:00).
Sea lions: 15, 30, 45, **60**, …
Parrots: 20, 40, **60**, …
The first common multiple of 15 and 20 is 60. 60 minutes after 10:00 is **11:00**.

questions.p: Question 7
questions.q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 9?
questions.e:
A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
1236 → 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 12 ✗ (divisible by 3 only)
4517 → 17 ✗
6024 → 12 ✗
2754 → 2 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 18 ✓
So **2754** (D). Check: 2754 ÷ 9 = 306.

questions.p: Question 8
questions.q: Which of these is a cube number?
questions.e:
Cube numbers: 1 × 1 × 1 = 1, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, 3 × 3 × 3 = **27**, 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
16 and 49 are square numbers, not cube numbers. 50 is neither. Answer B.

questions.p:
Question 9
In this sequence, each term is the position number squared, then subtract 1.
Position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
Term | 0 | 3 | 8 | 15
questions.q: What is the 9th term?
questions.e:
9th term = 9² − 1 = 81 − 1 = **80**.
Check the rule on the table: 4² − 1 = 16 − 1 = 15 ✓

questions.p:
Question 10
Pupils make a pattern of books on the library display shelves.
Position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
Number of books | 7 | 14 | 21 | 28
questions.q: (a) How many books are there in position 20?
questions.e:
Adding 7 each time is the same as multiplying the position by 7.
Rule: number of books = position × 7.
20 × 7 = **140**.
Common mistake: counting on 7 only once more (28 + 7 = 35), or doubling the 10th term from a wrong rule.

questions.p:
Question 10
Pupils make a pattern of books on the library display shelves.
Position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
Number of books | 7 | 14 | 21 | 28
questions.q:
(b) Sara says, "One of the positions has exactly 150 books."
Is Sara correct? Explain how you know.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No, with a correct reason, e.g. 150 is not a multiple of 7 / 150 ÷ 7 is not a whole number / 7 × 21 = 147 and 7 × 22 = 154, so 150 is between two terms. Do not accept "No" with no reason or an incorrect reason.
questions.e:
Every term is position × 7, so every term is a multiple of 7.
7 × 21 = 147 and 7 × 22 = 154. 150 is between them, so it is **not** a term. Sara is **not correct**.

questions.p:
Question 11
On the zoo trip there are b boys and g girls.
b + g = 42
questions.q: b = 19. What is the value of g?
questions.e:
b + g = 42 and b = 19, so 19 + g = 42.
g = 42 − 19 = **23**.
The letters stand for numbers that can change; here the total stays 42.

questions.p:
Question 12
At the zoo, the temperature inside the penguin house is −3 °C.
The temperature inside the reptile house is 28 °C.
questions.q: What is the difference between the two temperatures?
questions.e:
From −3 up to 0 is 3 degrees. From 0 up to 28 is 28 degrees.
3 + 28 = **31 °C**.
Common mistake: 28 − 3 = 25 (forgetting that −3 is below zero).

questions.p: Question 13
questions.q: What is the value of the digit 6 in the number 4.316?
questions.e:
4.316 = 4 ones + 3 tenths + 1 hundredth + 6 thousandths.
The 6 is in the thousandths column, so its value is **0.006** (6 thousandths).

questions.p: Question 14
questions.q: Work out 45 ÷ 1000
questions.e:
Dividing by 1000 moves every digit three places to the right (smaller).
45 → 4.5 (÷ 10) → 0.45 (÷ 100) → **0.045** (÷ 1000). Answer C.

questions.p: Question 15
questions.q:
(a) Ola says, "20/32 written in its simplest form is 10/16."
Is Ola correct? Tick (✓) Yes or No and explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No, with a correct explanation, e.g. 10 and 16 still have a common factor of 2 / 10/16 can be simplified again / the simplest form is 5/8. Do not accept "No" with no explanation.
questions.e:
**No.** 20/32 = 10/16 is correct, but 10/16 is **not** in its simplest form: 10 and 16 still share the factor 2.
10/16 = 5/8, and 5 and 8 have no common factor except 1, so the simplest form is **5/8**.
Quick way: divide by the highest common factor of 20 and 32, which is 4.

questions.p: Question 15
questions.q: (b) Work out 3/5 of 45

questions.p:
Question 16
In the school library, 2/5 of the books are fiction and 1/3 of the books are non-fiction.
The rest of the books are magazines.
questions.q: What fraction of the books are magazines? Show your working and give your answer in its simplest form.
questions.e:
Use a common denominator of 15.
2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15.
Fiction and non-fiction: 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15.
Magazines: 15/15 − 11/15 = **4/15**.
Mark scheme: M1 for 2/5 and 1/3 written with a common denominator (6/15 and 5/15) or 11/15 seen; A1 for 4/15 (oe).

questions.p: Question 17
questions.q: Work out 2/9 × 4
questions.e:
2/9 × 4 means 4 lots of 2/9: multiply the numerator by 4.
2 × 4 = 8, so the answer is **8/9**. (The denominator stays 9.)

questions.p: Question 18
questions.q:
Write <, > or = in each box.
0.7  ☐  3/4
40%  ☐  2/5
questions.e:
Change everything to decimals (or percentages).
3/4 = 0.75, and 0.7 = 0.70 is less than 0.75, so **0.7 < 3/4**.
2/5 = 4/10 = 0.4 = 40%, so **40% = 2/5**.

questions.q: Shade 35% of this grid.
questions.ms: 1 mark: exactly 7 of the 20 squares shaded (any 7 squares).
questions.e:
The grid has 5 × 4 = 20 squares, so each square is 100% ÷ 20 = 5%.
35% ÷ 5% = 7, so shade **7 squares** (any 7).
Check: 7/20 = 35/100 = 35%.

questions.p: Question 20
questions.q: Work out 7.3 − 2.86
questions.e:
Line up the decimal points and write 7.3 as 7.30.
7.30 − 2.86 = **4.44**.
Check: 4.44 + 2.86 = 7.30 ✓
Common mistake: 7.3 − 2.86 = 5.57 (lining the digits up from the right).

questions.p:
Question 21
The juice stall makes mango-orange juice.
It mixes mango juice and orange juice in the ratio 2 : 5
questions.q: The stall uses 6 cups of mango juice. How many cups of orange juice does it use?
questions.e:
2 : 5 is equivalent to 6 : ?
2 × 3 = 6, so multiply both parts by 3: 5 × 3 = **15 cups** of orange juice.
Ratio 2 : 5 = 6 : 15.

questions.p:
Question 22
The class trip to the zoo lasts 3.75 hours.
questions.q: 3.75 hours = 3 hours and how many minutes?
questions.e:
0.75 of an hour = 3/4 of 60 minutes = **45 minutes**.
So 3.75 hours = 3 hours 45 minutes.
Common mistake: 3 hours 75 minutes — the digits after the point are a decimal part of an hour, not minutes.

questions.q: Work out the size of angle x.
questions.e:
The angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
52° + 71° = 123°
x = 180° − 123° = **57°**.

questions.p: Question 24
questions.q:
Sketch a quadrilateral that has exactly one pair of parallel sides and two right angles.
Write the name of your shape.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a sketch of a right-angled trapezium (one pair of parallel sides, two right angles, the other two sides not parallel) AND the name trapezium. Accept recognisable misspellings. Do not accept a square, rectangle or parallelogram.
questions.e:
A **trapezium** has exactly one pair of parallel sides. If the side joining the two parallel sides is at right angles to them, the trapezium has two right angles (a right-angled trapezium).
Sketch: draw a long horizontal bottom side, a shorter horizontal top side starting above its left end, a vertical left side, and a slanting right side.
A rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles, so it is not correct.

questions.q: Which letter shows a radius of the circle?
questions.e:
A radius goes from the centre to the circumference: that is line **A**.
B passes through the centre from one side to the other, so it is a diameter. C does not pass through the centre (it is a chord). D points to the circumference (the curved edge).

questions.q: What is the order of rotational symmetry of the shape?
questions.e:
Trace the shape and turn the tracing around its centre. It fits on top of itself after a half turn (180°) and again after a full turn.
So it fits **2** times in a full turn: rotational symmetry of **order 2**.
Note: the shape has no lines of symmetry, but it still has rotational symmetry.

questions.p:

Question 28
A bag has 6 red counters and 2 blue counters. Ali takes one counter without looking.
questions.q: Which word best describes the chance that Ali takes a blue counter?
questions.e:
2 of the 8 counters are blue: 2/8 = 1/4. That is less than an even chance (1/2), but it can happen.
So it is **unlikely** (A). It is not impossible, because there are blue counters in the bag.

questions.p:
Question 29
A spinner has eight equal sections numbered 1 to 8. Rana spins it once.
questions.q: Explain why the events "the number is odd" and "the number is a multiple of 4" are mutually exclusive.
questions.ms: 1 mark: an explanation that the two events cannot happen at the same time because no number on the spinner is both odd and a multiple of 4, e.g. the multiples of 4 are 4 and 8, which are both even. Do not accept just "they cannot happen together" with no reference to the numbers.
questions.e:
Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7. Multiples of 4: 4, 8.
No number is in both lists (all multiples of 4 are even), so the two events **cannot happen at the same time**. Events like this are called mutually exclusive.

Question 30
Seven pupils write down how many library books they borrowed this term.
3,   5,   2,   5,   8,   4,   1
questions.q: What is the median number of books?
questions.e:
Put the numbers in order: 1, 2, 3, **4**, 5, 5, 8.
There are 7 numbers, so the median is the 4th one: **4**.
Common mistake: giving 5 (that is the mode) or taking the middle of the unordered list (5).

questions.e:

Triangle: 40 ÷ 2 = **20 m²**.

questions.p:
Question 32
Omar says, "Every number that is divisible by 3 is also divisible by 6."
questions.q: Give an example to show that Omar is wrong. Explain your example.
questions.ms: 1 mark: an odd multiple of 3 (e.g. 3, 9, 15, 21, 27, 33…) with a reason, e.g. 15 ÷ 3 = 5 but 15 is odd so it is not divisible by 6 / 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5. Do not accept an example that is a multiple of 6.
questions.e:
To be divisible by 6, a number must be divisible by 3 **and** be even.
Example: **9**. 9 ÷ 3 = 3, but 9 is odd, so 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5 is not a whole number.
One counter-example is enough to show that a statement is wrong.

Question 3
At sports day, seven pupils from Class 6A run 100 m. The table shows their times.
Name | Adam | Karim | Youssef | Omar | Ziad | Hamza | Seif
Time (seconds) | 15.42 | 14.87 | 16.05 | 15.20 | 14.87 | 15.80 | 15.66
For Class 6B the mean time is 15.90 seconds and the range is 0.62 seconds.
questions.q: Compare the times of Class 6A and Class 6B. Write two different comparisons.
questions.ms: 1 mark: Class 6A were faster on average, because their mean is lower (15.41 < 15.90) — FT their mean from Question 2. 1 mark: Class 6B's times were more consistent / closer together / less spread out, because their range is smaller (0.62 < 1.18); accept the range of 6A worked out as 1.18. Do not accept "6B is faster because 15.90 is bigger". Each comparison must refer to the mean or the range.
questions.e:
Mean: 6A = 15.41 s, 6B = 15.90 s. A **lower** time is faster, so **6A were faster on average**.
Range: 6A = 16.05 − 14.87 = 1.18 s; 6B = 0.62 s. 6B's range is smaller, so **6B's times were more consistent** (closer together).
Exam tip: compare one average AND one measure of spread, and say what each one means in the context.

questions.q: (d) Explain why a line graph is a good way to show this data.
questions.ms: 1 mark: temperature is continuous data / it changes all the time (between the readings), so joining the points shows how it changes over time and lets you read values between the times. Do not accept "it is easy to read" alone.
questions.e: Temperature is **continuous** data: it changes all the time, not only at 00:00, 03:00, … A line graph joins the readings, so it shows the **change over time** and lets you estimate temperatures between the readings (as in part (c)).

questions.p:
Question 5
The juice stall shows this price list.
Juice | Price of one cup
Orange | 18.50 pounds
Mango | 22.75 pounds
Guava | 15.25 pounds
questions.q:
Huda buys 3 cups of mango juice and 2 cups of guava juice. She pays with a 200-pound note.
How much change does she get? Show your working.
questions.e:
Mango: 3 × 22.75 = 68.25
Guava: 2 × 15.25 = 30.50
Total: 68.25 + 30.50 = 98.75
Change: 200 − 98.75 = **101.25 pounds**.
Mark scheme: M1 for 98.75 seen (or 200 − 3 × 22.75 − 2 × 15.25); A1 for 101.25. Accept 101.25 written as 101 pounds 25 piastres.

questions.p: Question 6
questions.q:
A jug holds 2.4 litres of orange juice. It is poured equally into 8 cups.
How much juice is in each cup?

questions.p: Question 7
questions.q:
The stall uses 6 mangoes to make 4 cups of mango juice.
How many mangoes does it need to make 18 cups?
questions.e:
The number of mangoes and the number of cups are in direct proportion.
4 cups need 6 mangoes, so 2 cups need 3 mangoes (halve both).
18 cups = 9 × 2 cups, so 9 × 3 = **27 mangoes**.
(Or: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 mangoes per cup; 18 × 1.5 = 27.)

questions.p: Question 8
questions.q:
On Friday the stall sells 240 cups of juice. 35% of them are orange juice.
How many cups of orange juice does it sell?

questions.p:
Question 9
152 pupils and 9 teachers go on a class trip to the zoo.
questions.q: (a) Each bus can carry 48 people. What is the smallest number of buses they need?
questions.e:
Number of people = 152 + 9 = 161.
161 ÷ 48 = 3.35…
3 buses carry only 144 people, so they need **4 buses**. Always round up when everyone must have a seat.
Common mistake: answering 3 or 3.35.

questions.p:
Question 9
152 pupils and 9 teachers go on a class trip to the zoo.
Zoo tickets cost 85 pounds for each pupil and 120 pounds for each teacher.
questions.q: (b) Work out the total cost of the tickets. Show your working.
questions.e:
Pupils: 152 × 85 = 12 920
Teachers: 9 × 120 = 1080
Total: 12 920 + 1080 = **14 000 pounds**.
Mark scheme: M1 for 152 × 85 + 9 × 120 (or 12 920 or 1080 seen with an attempt to add); A1 for 14 000.

questions.p: Question 10
questions.q:
The bus journey home takes 1.4 hours.
1.4 hours = 1 hour and how many minutes?
questions.e:
0.4 of an hour = 0.4 × 60 = **24 minutes**.
So 1.4 hours = 1 hour 24 minutes (not 1 hour 40 minutes).

questions.e:

Whole garden: 12 × 8 = 96 m².
Flower bed: 12 m² (from part a).
Vegetable bed: 5 × 3 = 15 m².
Grass: 96 − 12 − 15 = **69 m²**.

questions.q:
(c) The vegetable bed is shared between tomatoes and beans in the ratio 3 : 2
What area is used for tomatoes?
questions.e:
Vegetable bed = 15 m². The ratio 3 : 2 has 3 + 2 = 5 parts.
One part = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 m².
Tomatoes = 3 parts = 3 × 3 = **9 m²** (beans = 6 m²).

questions.ms: 1 mark: the correct reflection drawn. Counting squares from the bottom-left corner of the grid (across, up), the image has its vertices at (3, 1), (6, 1), (6, 2) and (4, 3). Accept a correct reflection drawn freehand if the vertices are clearly at these grid points.
questions.e:
The mirror line is diagonal. For each corner, count squares to the mirror line at right angles to it (diagonally) and go the same distance on the other side.
A quick way on this grid: label the bottom-left corner (0, 0). The shape's corners are (1, 3), (1, 6), (2, 6), (3, 4). Reflecting in this diagonal swaps the two numbers: (3, 1), (6, 1), (6, 2), (4, 3).
Join these points. The image should be the same size and shape, and flipped over the line.

Rotate the triangle 90° clockwise about the vertex C.
Draw the new triangle on the grid.
questions.ms: 1 mark: triangle drawn with vertices at (1, 1), (1, −2) and (3, 1). Do not accept a 90° anticlockwise rotation (vertices (1, 1), (1, 4), (−1, 1)).

C = (1, 1) stays where it is.

The side from C to (1, 3) goes 2 squares up. After a quarter turn clockwise it goes 2 squares **right**: to (3, 1).
New triangle: **(1, 1), (1, −2), (3, 1)**. Tip: use tracing paper, hold the pencil point on C and turn the paper a quarter turn clockwise.

Question 14
This shape is made from a cube with a square-based pyramid on top.

questions.q: How many faces does the shape have?
questions.e:
The cube has 6 faces, but its top face is covered by the pyramid: 5 faces show.
The pyramid has 5 faces, but its square base is on the cube: 4 triangles show.
5 + 4 = **9 faces**.
Common mistake: 6 + 5 = 11 (counting the two hidden faces where the shapes join).

questions.p: Question 15
questions.q: Sketch a net of a square-based pyramid.
questions.ms: 1 mark: one square and four triangles, arranged so that they fold into a square-based pyramid (e.g. a triangle on each side of the square). Do not accept a net with the wrong number of faces or with two triangles on the same side of the square.
questions.e:
A square-based pyramid has 1 square face and 4 triangular faces.
The usual net: a square in the middle with one triangle on each of its four sides (like a star).
Other nets also work, for example four triangles joined in a row (alternately pointing up and down) with the square attached to the base of one triangle.

questions.p: Question 16
questions.q: Which sentence describes capacity?
c: The amount of space that a solid object takes up
The amount that a container can hold when it is full
The total area of all the faces of a 3D shape
The distance all the way around a 2D shape
questions.e:
**Capacity** is how much a container can hold when it is full (for example 2 litres of juice) — answer B.
A describes volume. C describes surface area. D describes perimeter.

questions.p:
Question 17
Books are delivered to the library in a box shaped like a cuboid. It is 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm high.
questions.q: Work out the surface area of the box. Show your working.
questions.e:
A cuboid has three pairs of equal faces.
Top and bottom: 30 × 20 = 600, two of them = 1200
Front and back: 30 × 10 = 300, two of them = 600
Two ends: 20 × 10 = 200, two of them = 400
Surface area = 1200 + 600 + 400 = **2200 cm²**.
Mark scheme: M1 for at least two of 600, 300, 200 (or 1200, 600, 400) seen; A1 for 2200. Common mistake: 1100 (each face counted once) or 6000 (that is the volume).

questions.p: Question 18
questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 200" width="400" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16"><rect width="400" height="200" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="210" y1="175" x2="380" y2="175" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="210" y1="175" x2="105.3" y2="41" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M246,175 A36,36 0 0 0 187.8,146.6" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="235.4" y="128.9" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f1b33" font-style="italic" font-size="18">a</text><circle cx="210" cy="175" r="3" fill="#0f1b33"/></svg>
questions.q: Estimate the size of angle a.
questions.e:
Angle a is **obtuse**: it is more than a right angle (90°) but less than a straight line (180°). So 38° and 52° (acute) are wrong.
It is about a right angle plus 40° (90° + 40° = 130°), and still far from a straight line, so **128°** (A) is the best estimate. 152° would be much flatter, close to a straight line.

questions.p: Question 19
questions.q:
Hassan wants to draw a circle with a diameter of 9 cm using compasses.
How far apart should he set the point and the pencil of the compasses? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 4.5 cm with a reason, e.g. the compasses draw the radius / the radius is half of the diameter (9 ÷ 2 = 4.5). Do not accept 9 cm.
questions.e:
The distance between the compass point and the pencil is the **radius**.
Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 9 ÷ 2 = **4.5 cm**.
In the real test you may be asked to draw the circle: put the point on the centre, keep the setting at 4.5 cm and turn the compasses all the way round.

questions.p:
Question 20
At the zoo shop there is a game with a spinner showing four animals. Mona spins it 100 times. These are her results.
Animal | lion | zebra | monkey | giraffe
Frequency | 12 | 25 | 9 | 54
questions.q:
(a) Mona's friend says, "Each animal is equally likely."
Do Mona's results support this? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No, with a reason using the results, e.g. if each animal were equally likely each would come up about 25 times out of 100, but giraffe came up 54 times and monkey only 9 times. Do not accept "No" with no reason.
questions.e:
If the four animals were equally likely, each would land about 100 ÷ 4 = 25 times.
Giraffe came up 54 times (more than half) and monkey only 9 times. The results are far from 25 each, so they **do not support** the statement — the spinner seems more likely to land on giraffe.

questions.p:
Question 20
At the zoo shop there is a game with a spinner showing four animals. Mona spins it 100 times. These are her results.
Animal | lion | zebra | monkey | giraffe
Frequency | 12 | 25 | 9 | 54
questions.q: (b) Why is it better to spin the spinner 100 times than 10 times?
c: Each animal will then come up the same number of times
The results give a more reliable estimate of the probability
The spinner will land on giraffe every time
questions.e:
With only a few trials the results can be very different from what we expect, just by chance. A **large number of trials** gives a more reliable estimate of the probability (C).
More spins cannot change whether the spinner is fair (A), and the results will not become exactly equal (B).

questions.p:
Question 21
At the zoo shop there is a game with a spinner showing four animals. Mona spins it 100 times. These are her results.
Animal | lion | zebra | monkey | giraffe
Frequency | 12 | 25 | 9 | 54
questions.q: Mona spins the spinner another 200 times. About how many times should she expect it to land on zebra?
questions.e:
Zebra came up 25 times out of 100 (one quarter).
200 is double 100, so expect about 25 × 2 = **50 times**.

questions.p:
Question 22
Pupils collect different kinds of data on sports day.
questions.q: Which of these is continuous data?
c: the number of medals each class wins
the number of pupils in each race
the time each pupil takes to run 100 m
questions.e:
Continuous data is measured and can take any value in a range (time, length, mass, temperature).
Time to run 100 m (for example 15.42 s) is continuous — **D**.
Numbers of medals and pupils are discrete (counted). Favourite sport is categorical.

questions.p: Question 23
questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 440 244" width="440" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16"><rect width="440" height="244" fill="#ffffff"/><rect x="10" y="34" width="420" height="200" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="165" cy="134" r="86" fill="#eaf1fb"/><circle cx="275" cy="134" r="86" fill="#e3f4e5" fill-opacity="0.6"/><circle cx="165" cy="134" r="86" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="275" cy="134" r="86" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2"/><text x="140" y="24" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f1b33">factors of 24</text><text x="300" y="24" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f1b33">factors of 36</text></svg>
questions.q: Write the numbers 5, 8, 9, 12 and 18 in the correct places on the Venn diagram.
questions.ms: 1 mark for all five correct: 8 in 'factors of 24' only; 9 and 18 in 'factors of 36' only; 12 in the overlap; 5 outside both circles (inside the rectangle).
questions.e:
Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36.
**8** → factors of 24 only.
**9** and **18** → factors of 36 only.
**12** → a common factor, so it goes in the overlap.
**5** → a factor of neither, so it goes outside both circles.

questions.p:
Question 24
7 litres of juice are shared equally between 4 jugs.
questions.q: How many litres are in each jug? Give your answer as a mixed number or a decimal.
questions.e:
7 ÷ 4 = 7/4 (a fraction is a division of the numerator by the denominator).
7/4 = **1 3/4 litres** = 1.75 litres.

questions.p:
Question 25
A sequence starts at 2.5 and goes up by 0.75 each time.
2.5,   3.25,   4,   4.75,   …
questions.q: Is 10 a term in this sequence? Explain how you know.
questions.ms: 1 mark: Yes, with a correct reason, e.g. (10 − 2.5) ÷ 0.75 = 10 steps, a whole number / it is the 11th term / continuing the sequence 5.5, 6.25, 7, 7.75, 8.5, 9.25, 10. Do not accept "Yes" with no working.
questions.e:
From 2.5 to 10 is 10 − 2.5 = 7.5.
7.5 ÷ 0.75 = 10, a whole number of steps, so **yes**, 10 is in the sequence.
It is 10 steps after the first term, so it is the **11th term**.
Check by counting on: 4.75, 5.5, 6.25, 7, 7.75, 8.5, 9.25, 10 ✓

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Check every wrong answer.** Read the worked solution, then cover it and do the question again on paper until you can do it without help.
**Mark your written answers strictly.** Give yourself a mark only when your answer matches the mark scheme. For [2] questions, check whether your method would have earned the method mark (M1).
**Sort your mistakes:** a fact you did not know, a calculation slip, a misread question, a missing unit, or a graph or table read wrongly? Slips and misreading are the quickest marks to win back.

**Number lessons to revisit:** place value and regrouping → *Place Value and Decimals to Thousandths*; sequences and rules → *Counting On and Back and Negative Numbers* and *Sequences, Letters and Position-to-Term Rules*; long multiplication and division → *Multiplying Whole Numbers (up to 10 000 × 2-digit)* and *Dividing Whole Numbers (up to 1000 ÷ 2-digit)*; order of operations → *Order of Operations, Brackets and Laws of Arithmetic*; multiples, factors and divisibility → *Factors, Multiples and Tests of Divisibility*; cube numbers → *Square Numbers and Cube Numbers*; rounding → *Rounding Decimals*.

**Fractions, decimals and ratio:** *Fractions: Division, Operators and Simplest Form*, *Adding and Subtracting Fractions*, *Multiplying and Dividing Fractions by Whole Numbers*, *Fractions, Decimals and Percentages: Equivalence and Ordering*, *Adding, Subtracting, Multiplying and Dividing Decimals*, *Ratio and Direct Proportion*, and *Time: Decimals and Mixed Units*.

**Geometry:** *Angles: Measuring, Drawing and Angles in a Triangle*, *Quadrilaterals: Properties and Classification*, *Circles: Parts and Constructing Circles*, *Area of Rectangles and Right-angled Triangles*, *3D Shapes, Compound Shapes and Nets*, *Capacity, Volume and Surface Area*, *Coordinates in Four Quadrants*, *Rotational Symmetry, Translation, Reflection and Rotation*.

**Statistics and probability:** *Collecting and Representing Data*, *Mode, Median, Mean and Range, and Interpreting Data*, *Probability*. For explaining and convincing questions, reread *Checkpoint 6 Maths: The Test and How to Prepare*.
When you are ready, try **Practice Test 2** under timed conditions and compare your scores.
